tactical_explanations_en:
**A.** → True

A conjunction fails precisely when at least one conjunct fails.

$$\neg(p\wedge q)$$

$$\equiv \neg p\vee \neg q$$

$$\neg(p\wedge q)\leftrightarrow(\neg p\vee\neg q)$$

This is De Morgan's law for conjunction.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

Successor difference:

$$m=n+1$$

$$m-n=(n+1)-n$$

$$(n+1)-n=1$$

So the statement is True.

**C.** → False

Repeated roster entries do not create new elements of a set. Collapse duplicates first:

$$\{\alpha,\beta,\alpha\}=\{\alpha,\beta\}$$

Order is irrelevant as well:

$$\{\alpha,\beta\}=\{\beta,\alpha\}$$

Cardinality then counts distinct members only:

$$|\{\alpha,\beta,\alpha\}|=2$$

$$2\neq 3$$

The equality of rosters is correct, but the claimed cardinality $3$ is not.

So the statement is False.

**D.** → False

The intersection is removed once from each set's exclusive part.

$$
|A\setminus B| = 18-5 = 13
$$

$$
|B\setminus A| = 14-5 = 9
$$

$$
|A\triangle B| = 13+9 = 22\ne23
$$

The symmetric difference has size $22$.

So the statement is False.

**E.** → True

An implication can fail only when its antecedent is true and its consequent is false.

$$(p\rightarrow q)\wedge p = T\Longrightarrow p = T$$

$$p = T\ \text{and}\ p\rightarrow q = T\Longrightarrow q = T$$

$$((p\rightarrow q)\wedge p)\rightarrow q=T$$

No truth assignment makes the formula false.

So the statement is True.

$$R=(R\setminus F)\mathbin{\dot\cup}(R\cap F)$$

$$

$$

So the statement is False.

**C.** → True

A conjunction fails precisely when at least one conjunct fails.

$$\neg(p\wedge q)$$

$$\equiv \neg p\vee \neg q$$

This is De Morgan's law for conjunction.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → True

$$\forall x\,(N(x)\rightarrow O(x))$$

$$\forall x\,(O(x)\rightarrow\neg C(x))$$

Fix any $a$ with $N(a)$. Then

$$N(a)\Longrightarrow O(a)\Longrightarrow\neg C(a)$$

so every novelist fails $C$. The universal conclusion follows.

So the statement is True.

**E.** → True

The empty set can be listed as an element and is also a subset of every set. Membership:

$$\emptyset\in\{\emptyset,\{\emptyset\}\}$$

Subsethood is vacuous:

$$\forall z\,(z\in\emptyset\Longrightarrow z\in E)$$

$$\emptyset\subseteq E$$

Both uses of the empty set are valid.

So the statement is True.

tactical_explanations_en:
**A.** → False

Compare the formulas on an assignment where the antecedent holds and the consequent fails:

$$(p,q)=(T,F)$$

The original implication is

$$
p\rightarrow q = T\rightarrow F = F
$$

while the inverse is

$$
\neg p\rightarrow\neg q = F\rightarrow T = T
$$

The two truth values differ, so the inverse is not always equivalent to the original.

So the statement is False.

**B.** → False

A negative input supplies a counterexample because real squares are nonnegative.

$$x=-1\in\mathbb R$$

$$
\forall y\in\mathbb R,\qquad y^2\ge0 = -1\ \text{has no real solution}
$$

The universal claim fails at $x=-1$.

So the statement is False.

**C.** → False

Even and odd subset sizes split the full power set into equal halves.

$$
|\mathcal P(S)| = 2^5 = 32
$$

$$\#\{\text{even subsets}\}=\frac{32}{2}$$

$$\frac{32}{2}=16\ne15$$

There are $16$ even-cardinality subsets.

So the statement is False.

**D.** → False

Evaluating both sides reveals that the proposed placement of the intersection is not distributive. With $A=\{1\}$, $B=\{2\}$, $C=\{3\}$:

$$B\cap C=\emptyset$$

$$
A\cup(B\cap C) = \{1\}\cup\emptyset = \{1\}
$$

$$
(A\cup B)\cap C = \{1,2\}\cap\{3\} = \emptyset
$$

$$\{1\}\neq\emptyset$$

The two sides differ.

So the statement is False.

**E.** → False

A counterexample isolates the missing factor of $p\vee r$ in the proposed expression.

$$(p,q,r)=(T,F,F)$$

$$
p\vee(q\wedge r) = T\vee(F\wedge F) = T
$$

$$
(p\vee q)\wedge r = (T\vee F)\wedge F = F
$$

The formulas are not equivalent.

So the statement is False.

Members of a power set are subsets of the original set, not its bare symbols.

$$
